migrationNotes: Spine: one small shop's records grow from a café notebook to two linked tables, and at each stop we ask what a line stands for, what names it, and what to write when a fact is missing.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-rows-and-keys-9 (the old self-explanation). Its meaning is covered by the customer_id screen and by the skill check.

lesson.title: Know what a row represents

lead.text: Back to the notebook by the till. It works because every line means the same kind of thing: a line is a cup, and each line records the same facts about it, which are the day, the customer and the price. If the barista wrote a line for each cup on Monday and a line for each customer on Tuesday, nobody could add the pages up.

A database keeps its information in tables, and a table is the notebook page laid out as a grid. Each line becomes a row, and each fact becomes a column. A small shop might record its customers like this.

afterFigure.text: Each row in the grid is one customer. Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee have a row apiece, and every row carries the same three facts, which are the columns id, name and region. The code above the grid is a request to see those columns. Later lessons explain how to write requests like that, and for now it only matters what comes back.

Counting rows means counting the thing the table is about. If the café's notebook has one row per cup, a day's page holds as many rows as cups were sold, and the number of customers is a separate count. Every row also needs a name of its own, which is where we go next.

queries.label: Customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Names only
queries.sql: SELECT name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The café notebook has one line for every cup sold.

A row needs a name, because two rows can hold the same facts. Suppose a school keeps a list of its students, and two of them are both called Sam. If the only way to refer to a student were by name, nobody could say which Sam they meant.

The fix is a column that holds a different value in every row. A school would give each student a number and record it in a column called id. A column like that is called a primary key, because it names each row exactly once. In the shop's tables the primary key is always the column called id, so Ada is customer 1 and Ben is customer 2 whatever else about them changes.

Most columns are allowed to repeat. Two customers can live in the same region and the table is no worse for it. Only the key has to differ from row to row, and that matters in a moment, when a second table needs a way to point at a row of the first.
Names can repeat, so a table needs something else to tell its rows apart.

The shop now sells things, and a customer can place any number of orders. Writing every order into the customers table would repeat Ada's name and region each time, and the table would stop being about customers. So the shop starts a second table with one row for each order.

Here it is, with the customers beside it. Each order has an id of its own, from 101 to 106, and that id is the primary key of the orders table. The table also has to say whose order it was, and it does that with a column called customer_id, which holds the id of a row in customers.

afterFigure.text: Because one customer can place several orders, the same customer_id can turn up in more than one row of orders. Ada is customer 1, and her number can sit on any order she placed. That is allowed, because customer_id doesn't name the order. The order's own id does that.

So a column that holds another table's key can repeat, while a primary key can't. Following a customer through the shop means reading customer_id, and counting orders means counting rows of the orders table.

queries.label: Orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id, item, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Customers
queries.sql: SELECT id, name, region FROM customers ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each row of each table stands for one thing, and the id column names it.

queries.label: Ids and names
queries.sql: SELECT id, name FROM customers ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ids and references
queries.sql: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The orders.customer_id column stores the id of the customer who placed each order.

queries.label: Ada's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1 ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Ben's orders
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY id;

steps.headline: When a value is not known

lead.text: Order 106 was taken by phone. The customer confirmed the item, but nobody has agreed the price yet. The amount cell still has to hold something, and the obvious choice is 0. That would claim the order cost nothing, and every total of the amounts would then be wrong without anyone noticing.

Databases have a marker for exactly this situation. It is called NULL, and it means that there is no value in this cell because the value isn't known. NULL stands for the absence of a fact, which makes it a different thing from zero and from an empty piece of text. The picture shows where it sits in the orders table.

afterFigure.text: The difference matters most when you count or add. A total over the amounts should skip order 106, because no amount is recorded for it, instead of treating it as a free order. A later lesson shows exactly how a total deals with NULL. For now the point is that the table says honestly what it doesn't know.

queries.label: Unknown amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Known amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount IS NOT NULL ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Order 106 has no agreed price yet, so its amount cell has to say so.
Last, the shop gets another customer. Elm signs up today and hasn't ordered anything yet.

Think about which tables change. Elm is a new customer, so customers gains a row with the next free id. Elm has bought nothing, so orders is left exactly as it was. The two tables count different things, and each count follows the rows of its own table.

That is why a shop can have a different number of customers and orders, and why neither number says anything about the other. Whenever you count rows, first ask what one row of that table stands for, and count that.
The shop's customers table holds Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee.

lesson.orientation: Identify the thing each table row represents and keep missing values distinct from zero.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café keeps a notebook by the till. Every time someone buys a cup, the barista writes one line: the day, who bought it and what it cost. By Monday evening the page is full of short lines, and nobody has counted anything yet.

On Monday Mia bought three cups and Sam bought two. The owner wants to know how much was sold, and a few days later wants to know who comes in most often. Both answers are on the page, yet they come from counting different things. One counts cups and the other counts people.

Databases face the same choice all the time, and they store their information in much the same way as the notebook. This lesson follows a small shop's records as they grow. It starts with what one line stands for and how each line gets a name of its own, then asks what to write down when a fact isn't known.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say what one row stands for, and keep an unknown value apart from zero.

recap.keyIdea: A row stands for one thing and its primary key names it, so count rows by that thing, and record a missing value as NULL, never as 0.

blocks.text: Back at the notebook, the count followed the thing a line stands for. You counted 5 lines for Monday's cups, 2 order rows for customer 1 and 5 customers once Elm joined, and you gave an unknown price a marker of its own instead of writing 0.

recap.nextHook: The shop's orders table has six columns, and most questions need only two or three of them. The next lesson starts with a colleague who asks for exactly that: a short version of the table, with nothing deleted from the original.

questions.prompt: A shop keeps two tables, customers and orders. Which of them has one row for each order?
hints: Each table's id column names the thing its rows stand for. What do the ids in each table name?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The orders table has one row per order, identified by its order id. One customer can be associated with several of these order rows.

questions.onCorrect: orders. Its ids 101 to 106 name orders, so each row is one order, not one person.

misconceptions.feedback: That table holds one row per person. Look at which table's ids are the order numbers.

questions.prompt: How many rows of orders have customer_id = 1?
hints: Read customer_id, not the order's own id.
Look down the customer_id column for the value 1.
Count every row of orders that holds 1 in that column, and remember that one customer can have several.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Orders 101 and 102 reference customer 1; there are two.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Count rows by what customer_id holds. One customer can appear on several order rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts Ada once, as in customers. Count the order rows that point at her.

questions.prompt: The amount for order 106 is unknown. Which value records that in the table?
hints: Unknown and known to be zero make different claims.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NULL records a missing or unknown value. It does not mean an amount of zero or the text 'NULL'.

questions.onCorrect: NULL says the amount is missing. A 0 would claim the order was free, which is a different fact.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero is a known amount: it says the order cost nothing. Unknown is a different claim.
The orders table is not empty. Only one cell is missing.

questions.prompt: A shop's customers table holds Ada, Ben, Cy and Dee. Elm signs up and hasn't ordered anything yet. How many rows does customers hold now?
hints: Which table gets a row when a customer signs up?
Start from the customers already in the table.
Add the new customer to the four already there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four original customers plus Elm make five customer rows.

questions.onCorrect: 5. A new customer adds a row to customers only. Orders stay as they were.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before Elm joined. A new customer adds a row.

questions.prompt: Three customers each place two orders. How many rows should a one-row-per-order table have?
hints: Count orders rather than people.
Multiply the number of people by the orders per person.
Evaluate 3 × 2; each customer contributes two order rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three customers times two orders each makes six order rows.

questions.onCorrect: 6. One row per order: three customers with two orders each give 3 × 2 rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the customers. The table has a row for each order.
That adds 3 + 2. Each of the three customers contributes two rows, so multiply.

questions.prompt: Which column can repeat without making an order id ambiguous?
hints: Several orders can refer to the same customer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: orders.customer_id can repeat because one customer can place several orders. The separate order id still identifies each order uniquely.

questions.onCorrect: orders.customer_id can repeat. The order id stays unique, so each order is still named exactly once.

misconceptions.feedback: A primary key is different in every row, so it cannot repeat.
One of them can repeat: the one that points at a customer.

questions.prompt: A café notebook has one line for each cup sold. On Monday Mia bought 3 cups and Sam bought 2 cups. How many lines does Monday add to the notebook?
hints: What does one line in the notebook stand for?
Count cups, not people.
Put Mia's cups together with Sam's cups.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One line per cup: 3 cups for Mia and 2 for Sam make 5 lines.

questions.onCorrect: 5 lines. Each line is one cup, so the number of lines follows the cups and not the people.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the people. The notebook gets a line for each cup, not for each customer.

questions.prompt: A students table has two columns, id and name. Two students are both called Sam. Which column tells their rows apart?
hints: Which column could hold the same value in both rows?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: id. Each student has a different id, while both rows hold the same name.

questions.onCorrect: id. A primary key is different in every row, so it names the row even when other columns match.

misconceptions.feedback: Both rows hold Sam in name, so that column cannot tell them apart.

questions.prompt: Why do two rows of orders hold the same customer_id?
hints: Which column names each row of orders?

acceptedIdeas: Each order has its own id, and one customer can place several orders.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each order row has its own id, so two orders can still share one customer_id.

questions.onCorrect: One customer can place several orders. The order id keeps each row distinct.

choices.label: Each order has its own id, and one customer can place several orders.
One of the rows must be a mistake.
customer_id is the primary key of orders.

misconceptions.feedback: Repeating customer_id is allowed. The order id is what must differ from row to row.
The key of orders is id. customer_id only points at a customer.

questions.prompt: A table of amounts reads 20, 30, unknown, 10, with the unknown stored as NULL. How many orders have a known amount?
hints: Which of the four values is NULL?
NULL means no amount is recorded.
Take the unknown one away from the four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four orders, one with a NULL amount, leave three known amounts.

questions.onCorrect: 3. NULL marks the one amount nobody knows, so only the other three are known.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the NULL as if it were a known amount. NULL means the amount is not known.
